title: Kirsten Corazzini named UNH senior executive director of healthcare strategy - NH Business Review
content: Kirsten Corazzini, dean of the University of New Hampshire’s College of Health and Human Services, has been named Senior Executive Director of Healthcare Strategy at UNH, effective Jan. 2, 2027. In her new role, Corazzini will direct the University System of New Hampshire’s GO-NORTH Rural Health Transformation Workforce Hub, a five-year initiative with funding of up to $97 million to strengthen healthcare workforce education and expand access to training in rural communities. She will oversee investments in clinical simulation training, expand educational pathways into healthcare professions, and develop partnerships to address workforce shortages, particularly in rural and underserved communities throughout New Hampshire. Corazzini joined UNH in 2022 and has led significant growth in the College of Health and Human Services’ academic programs, research, and statewide partnerships. Among her accomplishments was establishing UNH’s School of Nursing, which now serves approximately 800 students and whose undergraduate program recently earned a place among the nation’s top 100 in U.S. News & World Report’s rankings. She also led the expansion of the college’s research infrastructure and strengthened partnerships with Dartmouth University and Dartmouth Health, and Mass General Brigham. Under her leadership, the college advanced from unranked to a top-10 position among Schools of Allied Health in New England for National Institutes of Health funding. Corazzini will continue serving as dean of CHHS through the transition to her new role in January. title: TD Cowen backs UnitedHealth & Humana with buy upgrades, shares rise - TradingView
content: Shares of UnitedHealth UNH and Humana HUM ticked up in premarket trading on Friday after TD Cowen upgraded both health insurers to ‘Buy’ from ‘Hold’, citing an improved outlook and scope for further upside. Target price on UNH raised to $455 from $402, which implies a 38% increase from last closing price. For UnitedHealth UNH, TD Cowen analyst Ryan Langston sees the stock as an attractive story, with a credible path toward mid-high-teens EPS growth through 2028. “We see a credible path toward mid-high-teens EPS growth through at least 2028 given Medicare Advantage benefit design, Optum Health recovery & Commercial/Medicaid improvement”. The brokerage notes that recent CRUSH proposals and potential for further regulatory/congressional impact are important near-term debates. Additionally, TD Cowen said continued external growth at Optum Rx and commercialization of Optum Insight’s AI-first products are areas to watch. For Humana on the other hand, Langston sees a relatively clear path towards a meaningful step-up in 2027 EPS growth and a greater than $40 EPS in 2028. “Our 2027 MA benefits analysis suggests major carriers, including HUM, broadly prioritized profitability recovery over enrollment for 2027, reducing the risk that HUM is competitively disadvantaged by its pricing actions,” the analyst noted. Sees potential for HUM to raise its prior operating leverage framework at its Dec. 10 investor update, as it lifted PT to $485 from $430, which implies a 28% increase from last closing price. HUM was about ~2% before the opening bell. title: UnitedHealth UNH Stock Dives 20% as Breakup Pressure and Medicare Audit Threats Hit the Healthcare Insurers - FXLeaders
content: UnitedHealth UNH stock plunged to $320s as proposed Medicare audit reforms, political calls to break up healthcare conglomerates and rising medical costs threaten insurers’ earnings and margins. Healthcare stocks extended their decline on Wednesday after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed tougher oversight of Medicare, Medicaid, the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) and the health insurance marketplace. UnitedHealth Group (NYSE: UNH) has been among the hardest hit, falling approximately 20% in three sessions and slipping below $330. Proposed Medicare Advantage audit reforms, political pressure to break up large healthcare conglomerates and rising medical costs are combining to undermine investor confidence in the sector. A major catalyst emerged on November 16, when CMS proposed the Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare, or CRUSH rule. The proposal would formalise risk-adjustment data validation audits and allow regulators to extrapolate findings from sampled claims across entire Medicare Advantage contracts. Audits could extend back to payment year 2018, with CMS estimating that the framework could recover approximately $9 billion annually across the industry. UnitedHealth faces considerable exposure because it operates the country’s largest Medicare Advantage business. Mizuho analyst Ann Hynes identified UnitedHealth and Humana as the insurers most vulnerable to the proposed changes, followed by CVS Health, Elevance Health, Centene and Molina Healthcare. Political pressure is creating another headwind. Senator Elizabeth Warren has called for breaking up vertically integrated healthcare conglomerates, specifically naming UnitedHealth, CVS and Cigna while supporting the proposed Break Up Big Medicine Act. Restrictions on insurers owning pharmacy benefit managers and healthcare providers could threaten UnitedHealth’s integrated Optum business model. Such measures could limit operational flexibility, increase compliance costs and potentially weaken the advantages of its vertically integrated structure. UnitedHealth shares have come under renewed selling pressure, falling approximately 9% on Wednesday after failing to consolidate gains above $400. The stock has retreated into the $320s, with investors reassessing the regulatory and operational risks facing the managed-care sector. Insurers are also facing elevated medical utilisation, particularly across outpatient and specialty services. If healthcare costs continue rising faster than premiums, underwriting profitability could deteriorate, adding pressure to earnings forecasts. UnitedHealth retains significant scale and cash-flow generation, but the combination of regulatory uncertainty, potential Medicare payment recoveries and higher medical costs leaves its shares vulnerable. Investors will be watching management guidance and the $350 area as an important technical reference, while a sustained recovery will likely require greater clarity on the potential financial impact of the CMS proposal.

title: Huskies Drop Game 1 vs. UNH - University of Connecticut Athletics
content: STORRS, Conn. — UConn men's hockey dropped game one of the two game series vs. New Hampshire by a final of 6-3 Thursday evening. The Huskies scored once in each period and finished with a 25-22 shot advantage, including a power-play goal in the second. UConn opened the first period a man down when Brendan Dunphy was called for a hooking penalty early in the first period. New Hampshire broke through five minutes in when a shot from the point beat Hendrickson. On the ensuing shift, Ethan Gardula found the back of the net following a Joey Muldowney steal, tying the game at one. Following the tie, both teams traded chances, but New Hampshire regained the lead when a save by Hendrickson bounced to a New Hampshire skater who fired it home for the 2-1 lead. The Huskies started the second period strong looking for the equalizer, but New Hampshire defense stayed strong. The Wildcats increased their lead early in the second when the Wildcats beat the Huskies defense creating an odd man rush. The Huskies answered on the power play shortly after when Alexandre Blais fired a one timer cutting the deficit to 3-2. The Huskies increased the pressure and were able to create another power play opportunity, but the Huskies were unable to find the back of the net with the man advantage. With the power play expiring, New Hampshire stole the puck at the blue line, and another odd man rush gave the Wildcats their fourth goal of the night once again giving the Wildcats the two-goal lead. The two teams battled in the third, but New Hampshire found the back of the net first increasing the lead to 5-2. Freshman Lirim Amidovski answered for UConn late in the period cutting the deficit to two. With under three minutes remaining in the game, UConn pulled Hendrickson in favor of an extra skater but with 53 seconds left in the game the Wildcats scored on the empty net securing the 6-3 win. title: UNH Poll Finds Voters Happy With NH Elections, Boosting Case to Keep Scanlan - NH Journal
content: Republican Secretary of State David Scanlan says performance, not partisanship, should be the criteria for filling his office. And new numbers from the UNH Survey Center show Granite Staters are very happy with Scanlan’s performance as the state’s top election official. The latest Granite State Poll, a States of Opinion Project, released Thursday, found 88% of voters said casting a ballot in the Nov. 3 election was “very easy.” That includes 84% of registered Democrats and 89% of undeclared voters. More than half of Granite Staters said voting took them less than 15 minutes on Election Day, and 75% said they were very confident in the accuracy of the vote count. “I believe this information represents that the substantial efforts that my office has been taking to build voter confidence in elections is working,” Scanlan told NHJournal. The findings arrive as Scanlan seeks another term from a legislature transformed from a solid GOP majority to a 292-seat Democratic House supermajority, and a 15-9 majority in the Senate. Lawmakers will elect the secretary of state in a joint session on Organization Day, Dec. 2. Three Democrats have entered the race to replace him: NH-01 candidate and Hampton Select Board Chair Carleigh Beriont; James Butler, who worked for America Votes, a national progressive political organization; and Manchester state Rep. Patrick Long. “I’m seeking this office on the basis of my own record, and it’s a strong one,” Scanlan said Tuesday when announcing his reelection bid. Three prominent Democrats are backing him: former U.S. ambassadors Dick Swett, George Bruno and Terry Shumaker, who served under Democratic presidents. “It would be tragic for New Hampshire if Democrats turned this office into a political football,” they said in a statement Thursday. Political observers say Scanlan holding on to his job is a long shot at best. The warning accompanying their endorsement was blunt. “It would be tragic for New Hampshire if Democrats turned this office into a political football. It’s important not to overreach.” Their support adds to an argument Scanlan and his allies have been making since the election: A change in the legislature’s partisan control should not automatically mean a change in the office responsible for administering elections. The UNH findings offer support for Scanlan’s argument. Among self-identified Democrats who voted, 96% said they were very confident their ballot was counted accurately, with another 3% somewhat confident. Democratic confidence exceeded that of independents and Republicans. Among Republicans, whose party suffered sweeping losses, 54% were very confident and 29% somewhat confident their vote was counted accurately. Among independents, the figures were 59% and 32%, respectively. Scanlan, who became secretary of state in 2022, previously spent two decades as deputy to Democrat Bill Gardner. Gardner held the office for 46 years, surviving changes in legislative control and winning support from both parties. The three Democrats seeking the office are campaigning on pledges to adopt or support new election policies supported by the political left, such as expanded voting by mail and no-excuse absentee balloting. Scanlan’s allies point to his refusal to turn over confidential voter information to President Donald Trump’s Justice Department as evidence of independence from his party. There is also the question of who will defend New Hampshire’s first-in-the-nation presidential primary against pressure from national party leaders. Beriont and Butler have pledged to protect it. Scanlan argues his experience makes him best equipped to withstand that pressure. Former Democratic state Rep. Jim Splaine, who authored the 1975 law protecting the primary’s status, is also backing Scanlan. For Scanlan, the challenge is translating confidence in the elections into votes from Democratic lawmakers. His stated standard for running the office applies regardless of which party controls the State House: “The law is the law.” With progressive politics on the rise, however, that may not be enough. A sign pointing out the sights and sounds visitors might encounter at College Woods in New Hampshire helped improve their moods, a University of New Hampshire researcher found. “There’s a huge body of evidence saying being in nature is good for us,” said Lauren Ferguson, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the University of New Hampshire’s Department of Recreation Management and Policy. Ferguson conducted research at College Woods in New Hampshire to study how walking outdoors affects people’s feelings. “What I did find is that the perception of biodiversity is more important than the actual biodiversity,” Ferguson said. She found that simply placing a sign at the entrance to College Woods listing the sights and sounds visitors might encounter had a positive effect on their moods. Ferguson said people’s perceptions of their surroundings mattered more than the specific sights they encountered. The sign also made visitors more aware of their surroundings by telling them what to look for, making the experience more restorative. “Our normal day-to-day life is extremely cognitively depleting, but being in a place like this allows your brain to still remain focused and remain engaged while you’re also simultaneously recovering from that fatigue,” Ferguson said. Ferguson said the biggest positive effects were seen during warmer months, but nature walks can improve mood in any season. She encourages people to take walks outdoors, even during colder months. content: UnitedHealth Group (NYSE: UNH) stock has fallen back below $350s as proposed Medicare Advantage audit reforms, political pressure to break up healthcare conglomerates and rising medical costs intensify concerns about earnings and margins. UnitedHealth shares have come under renewed selling pressure, falling approximately 9% on Wednesday after failing to consolidate gains above $400. The stock has retreated into the $350s, with investors reassessing the regulatory and operational risks facing the managed-care sector. A major catalyst emerged on November 16, when the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services proposed the Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare, known as the CRUSH rule. The proposal would formalise risk-adjustment data validation audits and allow regulators to extrapolate findings from sampled claims across entire Medicare Advantage contracts. Audits could reach back to payment year 2018, while CMS estimates the framework could recover approximately $9 billion per year across the industry. UnitedHealth faces significant exposure because it operates the country’s largest Medicare Advantage business. Mizuho analyst Ann Hynes identified UnitedHealth and Humana as the insurers most affected by the proposed changes, followed by CVS Health, Elevance Health, Centene and Molina Healthcare. Plitical pressure is adding another challenge. Senator Elizabeth Warren has called for breaking up vertically integrated healthcare conglomerates, specifically naming UnitedHealth, CVS and Cigna and citing the proposed Break Up Big Medicine Act. Restrictions on insurers owning pharmacy benefit managers and healthcare providers could threaten UnitedHealth’s integrated Optum business model, potentially reducing operational flexibility and creating additional regulatory costs. Elevated medical utilisation, particularly in outpatient and specialty services, is also weighing on insurers’ margins. If healthcare costs rise faster than premiums, underwriting profitability could deteriorate further. Although UnitedHealth retains substantial scale and cash-flow generation, regulatory uncertainty and medical-cost pressures leave the stock vulnerable. Investors will watch management guidance and the $350 support area closely as the company faces growing challenges to its earnings outlook.

He had made a similar trade last week, doubling his Nasdaq-100 put position when the index bounced from around 27,000. He also bought back some puts on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) after trimming the bet. Burry went into Nvidia’s (NVDA) earnings holding $140 puts expiring in February 2027 and passed on buying short-dated calls to cushion the bet. After the results, he said he planned to spend less time covering Nvidia, but one number stood out. Days sales outstanding, a measure of how long it takes to collect payment, rose to 64 days from 60. Customers owed Nvidia $81 billion at quarter-end, as quarterly revenue more than doubled from a year earlier to $115.8 billion. “Without Jensen there I wonder how this improves - customers will find it harder to pay, or will just take more time to pay, I imagine,” Burry said, referring to former CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia attributed the increase to the timing of Rubin chip shipments and longer payment terms for some investment-grade customers. Burry also flagged the wait for Nvidia’s 10-Q, which interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress said would arrive in the coming weeks. Give me that afternoon back every week and I’ll gladly write that check every month,” the reader said. Burry agreed that kind of tool was coming. He said that businesses could run smaller models on their own machines, using their own records. Nvidia already makes hardware for the market. Its Nemotron 3.5 Bolt model can run on GeForce RTX graphics cards. Meanwhile, Tencent accounted for just over 2% of Burry’s portfolio earlier this month. The company subsequently reported negative quarterly free cash flow of 69.1 billion yuan. “It is concerning and the main reason I have not added. He also questioned whether bargain hunters in private credit were moving too soon. “I've heard capital is already being mobilized to pick at depressed private credit. Could be a self-fulfilling prophecy, but if the size of the AI boom's bust is large enough at the data center level, moves today would likely be overwhelmed and proven early,” he said. Burry also explained why his buy target for Netflix (NFLX) had fallen to the high $30s. In July, he had put the low $50s just outside his buying range and questioned the staying power of its hits. “Disney produces wine. Netflix produces milk,” he said at the time. In the latest chat, Burry said streaming rivals had caught up. “The process of producing hit shows has been a fraught exercise for a long time, and reality TV is a sign of rot in that creative process. It is the cheap more certain option, but one that does not breed network loyalty,” he said. Burry was equally open about Ero Copper (ERO). In September, he saw a mismatch that favored the miner. Data centers could lift copper demand within two or three years, while new deposits could take about 18 years to reach production. “My investment in ERO was ill-timed. I still own it in small size but have not added but once,” he said in the latest chat. “I will continue to evaluate it but I think this one has more to it than the AI trade. As I said it is not often I get bullish on a miner.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Andrew Ross Sorkin, a columnist for The New York Times, raised a question DealBook readers had repeatedly asked about whether a merger should trigger Musk’s Tesla stock awards. “I should not receive those stock option awards simply for merging with SpaceX because that is not meeting the deal, which was that I should only get those stock options for Tesla performance, not just because of a merger,” Musk said. A merger could change how Musk earns his Tesla pay. He called the awards stock options, though Tesla’s filings say his 2025 package consists of 423.7 million shares of performance-based restricted stock. To earn each of the 12 installments, Tesla typically must hit an operating goal and a valuation target, starting at $2 trillion and rising to $8.5 trillion. If the deal’s structure triggered Tesla’s change-in-control clause, shares Musk had already earned would vest. The deal price would factor into Tesla’s valuation, which alone would determine whether he earned more. One way the clause could kick in is if a new owner gained more than half of Tesla’s voting power. An exception applies if Tesla’s existing shareholders keep at least half the voting power in Tesla or its parent company, with their stakes in about the same proportion as before. To work out what Musk earned, Tesla would use whichever is higher: its last closing price or the price shareholders received in the deal. A higher deal could unlock more shares for Musk even if Tesla missed an operating goal. He would give up any part of the award he still had not earned when the deal closed. “If you’d asked me five years ago, do I ever think there’s any purpose in SpaceX and Tesla getting together, I would have said no,” Musk said. Tesla develops AI for self-driving cars and its Optimus robot, while SpaceX builds large AI models and supplies computing power to customers such as Anthropic. The case for a merger hinges on whether they could create more value for shareholders together. “These require shareholder votes, which may or may not succeed,” Musk said. He added that his own vote would have to take into account whether the terms made financial sense for other SpaceX investors. Musk confirmed last month that both companies had formed committees of independent directors to explore a deal. title: Why Is UnitedHealth Stock Falling? - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036? UnitedHealth Group (UNH) stock fell 5.4% on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 1.0%. There was no announcement, earnings report or filing from the company. A market commentary published that day said the shares fell amid renewed regulatory scrutiny. All seven other managed health care companies worth $2 billion or more fell too. Management’s comments on its October earnings call, weeks before the fall, show which parts of UnitedHealth’s business sit closest to regulators. By management’s own account, rules set outside the company affect both its government plans and its commercial business. On its October 13 call, management said policy-driven regulatory developments continue to reshape the industry. In Medicaid, UnitedHealth works with states on rates that reflect the impacts of regulatory actions. Management said the timing of those updates remains uneven. The company expects 2026 to be the low point for core Medicaid margins. It expects those margins to come in moderately better than a 1% loss. In the commercial business, management pointed to the dispute process under the No Surprises Act. It said a small number of clinician groups and third-party organizations abuse that process. Arbitration awards can reach nearly 6% of total medical spend in some regions, management said. UnitedHealth has little room to absorb such costs. The company recorded a net margin of 3.5% over the twelve months to September 2026, down from 4.0% a year earlier. Did UnitedHealth Fall With Other Managed Care Companies? Yes, and it fell further than any of them. All seven other companies worth $2 billion or more in its managed health care sub-industry fell on Tuesday, logging a median drop of 3.9%. Just one of them fell 5% or more: Molina Healthcare, down 5.1%. Every company on UnitedHealth’s peer list fell as well, among them Humana, down 3.9%. The broader health care sector fell less, with the sector fund XLV down 1.4%. UnitedHealth moved with its group, and its drop was larger than the group’s median. A fall this large is rare for UnitedHealth. Only one other session in the prior year brought a fall at least this big: a 19.6% drop on January 27, 2026. Over the past twelve months, the stock returned 24.3%, against 10.3% for the S&P 500. Shares climbed from a 52-week closing low of $259.02 on March 27 to a high of $436.35 on July 21. Tuesday’s close of $389.68 left the stock below that high. UnitedHealth trades at 0.78 times its sales over the past twelve months, against 3.2 times for the S&P 500. UnitedHealth is expected to report its fourth-quarter 2026 results in January 2027. The number to watch is the medical care ratio, the share of premiums spent on care, which the company put at 88.4% for the third quarter. Tuesday showed how one stock can drop with its whole group on a day its company announced nothing. Holding on is easier when your portfolio falls less than the market. title: UnitedHealth Stock (UNH) Falls 5.4% on CMS Audit Proposal (Nov 17) - Gotrade
content: Gotrade News - In the latest UnitedHealth stock news, shares of UnitedHealth (UNH) fell 5.42% to close at $389.68 on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, a drop of $22.34 from the previous close of $412.02. Financial media tied the slide in UnitedHealth stock to a federal proposal that would widen audits of Medicare Advantage plans and reach back to payment year 2018. Regular-session close on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, 4:00 p.m. New York time. Stock prices: Yahoo Finance, cross-checked against the closing price on Nasdaq.com. Volume and 30-day average volume: Nasdaq.com. 52-week range: Yahoo Finance daily highs and lows since November 18, 2025. Indices: Yahoo Finance daily closes for the same date. 10-year Treasury yield: U.S. Treasury daily par yield curve for the same date. Follow UNH's latest price on our UnitedHealth (UNH) stock price today page. The stock opened at $399.23, well below Monday's close, and never got back to that level during the day. It traded between $387.14 and $399.99 and finished just $2.54 above the session low. Volume reached 8.0 million shares, 39.50% above the 5.8 million share average. The decline was far steeper than the broader market. The Nasdaq Composite fell 0.74% to 24,328.38, the S&P 500 lost 1.03% to 7,340.53 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.64% to 50,759.42, leaving UnitedHealth 4.68 percentage points behind the Nasdaq. The US 10-year Treasury yield fell 2.0 basis points to 5.10%. Elsewhere in health care, Eli Lilly (LLY) slipped 1.13% and Novo Nordisk (NVO) fell 2.16%. After the drop, the stock sits 15.58% below its 52-week high of $461.62 and 52.24% above its 52-week low of $255.97, with a market value of $349.2 billion. On November 16, federal health officials proposed a rule called CRUSH, short for Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare, that would expand Medicare Advantage audits, according to GuruFocus. The rule would codify risk adjustment data validation audits without a fee-for-service adjuster and extrapolate the findings starting with payment year 2018. CMS estimates the approach would recover about $9 billion per payment year on average, and comments are due January 19, 2027. GuruFocus described extrapolation as the key change, because a coding error found in a sample can be multiplied across an entire contract. As reported by TIKR, CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz framed the rule as a way to "crush fraud, waste, and abuse," while UnitedHealth, the largest Medicare Advantage insurer, has not sized the potential hit. Managed care peers Humana and CVS Health also traded lower, GuruFocus reported. Per 24/7 Wall St., the selling also followed a call by Sen. Elizabeth Warren to break up major health care conglomerates, in which she named UnitedHealth alongside two other vertically integrated insurers. UnitedHealth issued no press release on the day, the outlet noted. Management has promised to give its 2027 outlook before year-end, according to TIKR.
